<x_0.0264><y_0.0844>ERECTION, in a general fenfe, the art of railing or e- levating any thing, as the ereclion of a perpendicular, &c. It is alfof ufed in a figurative fenfe, as the erecction of a bithopric, marquifate, &c.<x_0.8486><y_0.143><class_Text>

<x_0.0234><y_0.1688>EREMIT. See HERMIT.<x_0.4375><y_0.1836><class_Text>

<x_0.0225><y_0.1828>EREMITA, in zoology. See SCARABNUS.<x_0.7061><y_0.1992><class_Text>

<x_0.0215><y_0.1969>ERFURT, a large and beautiful city of Upper Saxony in Germany, capital of Thuringia, and fubject to the elefor of Mentz: E. long. 11° 6', N. lat. 51°.<x_0.8467><y_0.2414><class_Text>

<x_0.0205><y_0.2383>ERGOT, in farriery, is a flub, like a piece of foft horn, about the bignefs of a chefnut, placed behind and be- low the pattern-joint, and commonly hid under the tuft of the fetlock.<x_0.8457><y_0.2953><class_Text>

<x_0.0195><y_0.2945>ERICA, or HEATH, in botany. a genus of the ochan- dria monogynia clafs. The calix conflts of four leaves, and the corolla of four legments; the filaments are inferred into the receptacle; the antherx are bifid; and the capfule has four cells. There are thirty-eight species, five of which are natives of Britain, viz the vulgaris, or common heath; the cinerea, or fine-leaved heath; the tetralix, or crofs-leaved heath; the cilia-ris, or rough-leaved heath; and the multiflora, or fir-leaved health.<x_0.8477><y_0.4359><class_Text>

<x_0.0186><y_0.4344>ERIDANUS, in altronomy. See Vol. I. p. 487.<x_0.7754><y_0.4516><class_Text>

<x_0.0176><y_0.4492>ERIE, a vaft lake to the weflward of Penfilvania, in North America, fituated between 80° and 87° W. long, and between 41° and 42° N lat.<x_0.8438><y_0.4938><class_Text>

<x_0.0166><y_0.4914>ERIGERON, or SWEET FLA BANE, in botany, a genus of the fyngencfia polygamia fuperflua clafs. The receptacle is naked; the pappus is liairy; and the ca-dii of the corolla are linear and very narrow. There are fixteen fpecies, two of which are natives of Britain, viz. the acre, or blue-flowered flea-bane; and the ca-nadenfe, or Canada flea-bane.<x_0.8447><y_0.5914><class_Text>

<x_0.0156><y_0.5891>ERINACEUS, or Hedge-hog, in zoology, a genus of quadrupeds belonging to the order of ferae, the characters of which are thefe : they have two foreteeth in the upper-jaw, at a conferable diflance from one another, and two in the under jaw, lefs diflant; and they have two recumbent dog-teeth, one on each fide. There are three fpecies, viz. 1. The europeus, or common hedge-hog, with round ears, and crefted no-frils. It is about nine inches long; the upper part of the body is totally covered with sharp prickles, and the under part is covered with hair. The hedge-hog, even when flanding on his legs, has a very ugly affect. His body is an oblong mafs, convex above, terminated on the fore-part by a very harp muzzle, and mounted on four floor legs, of which nothing appears but the feet, and the tail is not discernible. His ears are broad, round, and thort; and his eyes are fmall and protuberant. The length of his body, from the point of the muzzle to the anus, is about nine inches.<x_0.8428><y_0.8578><class_Text>

<x_0.0479><y_0.8562>The hedge-hog has a very uncommon method of defending himself from the attacks of other animals: being poffelfed of little strength or agility, he does not attempt to fly from or affail his enemies; but ereclts his brillies, and rolls himself up like a ball, expoing no<x_0.8418><y_0.9305><class_Text>
